name: carrymem
description: Your portable AI memory layer — preferences, decisions, and corrections that follow you across models, tools, and devices. Classify, store, and recall what matters using zero-LLM rule-based classification (88% coverage), SQLite with FTS5 full-text search, and cross-client MCP integration for Cursor, Claude Code, TRAE, Windsurf, Cline, and more.

tools.name: classify_message
tools.description: Analyze a user message and classify it into one of 7 memory types: user_preference (⭐), correction (🔧), decision (🎯), fact_declaration (📌), relationship (❓), task_pattern (🔄), or sentiment_marker (💭). Returns {type, confidence, should_remember} where should_remember is false for noise/sentiment. Uses zero-LLM rule engine (88% of messages classified without any API call). Idempotent: classifying the same message twice returns identical results. Use this when you need to understand what kind of information the user is sharing before deciding whether to store it.

tools.name: get_classification_schema
tools.description: Return CarryMem's complete classification schema: all 7 memory types with their icons, descriptions, examples, confidence thresholds, and type weights used for importance scoring. Returns a structured JSON schema that explains how the classifier works. Read-only and idempotent. Use this when you need to explain the classification system to the user or debug why a message was classified a certain way.

tools.name: batch_classify
tools.description: Classify multiple messages in a single call. Accepts an array of messages and returns classifications for each. More efficient than calling classify_message individually when processing conversation history, batch imports, or multiple user statements. Each message is independently classified using the same zero-LLM rule engine. Returns array of {message, type, confidence, should_remember} objects. Idempotent.

tools.name: classify_and_remember
tools.description: Classify a user message into one of 7 memory types AND store it if it contains memorable information (should_remember=true). This is the primary entry point for storing memories. The full pipeline: auto-classify → coreference resolution → auto-redaction (blocks API keys/passwords) → validate → store with importance scoring. Returns {should_remember, type, content, entries, stored, storage_keys, summary} with the number of entries stored. NOT idempotent: re-classifying an already-stored message may create duplicates (use consolidate_memories later). Always prefer this over separate classify + remember calls. Use when the user shares personal preferences, makes decisions, corrects previous statements, or states facts about themselves.

tools.name: recall_memories
tools.description: Search stored memories using semantic full-text search (FTS5) across all memory types. Supports filtering by namespace, memory_type, time range, and confidence threshold. Results are ranked by relevance score with cross-language support (English/Chinese/Japanese). By default updates access timestamps on recalled memories (affects importance scoring). Returns array of {key, content, type, confidence, namespace, created_at, updated_at} objects. Empty array means no matches found. Read-only operation. Use when the user asks about their past statements, preferences, decisions, or any previously shared information.

tools.name: forget_memory
tools.description: Permanently delete a specific memory by its key or ID. Destructive operation: the memory cannot be recovered after deletion (unless restored from backup). The memory's version history is also removed. Requires exact memory_key as parameter. Returns boolean success status. Use with caution — confirm with the user before forgetting unless explicitly requested. Use when the user wants to remove incorrect, outdated, or unwanted stored information.

tools.name: index_knowledge
tools.description: Scan and index knowledge base files from the configured Obsidian vault (or other knowledge adapter). Parses markdown files, extracts frontmatter metadata (tags, aliases, categories), builds FTS5 search index, and stores entries in the knowledge base. This is a potentially slow operation for large vaults (thousands of files). Idempotent: re-indexing updates existing entries. Returns {indexed_count, skipped_count, errors, duration}. Use when: (1) after adding new files to vault, (2) first-time setup, (3) user reports stale knowledge results. Does NOT require parameters — uses pre-configured vault path.

tools.name: recall_from_knowledge
tools.description: Search the indexed knowledge base (Obsidian vault notes, documentation files) using FTS5 full-text search. Separate from recall_memories which searches user conversation memories. Returns array of {source_file, content, title, tags, relevance_score} objects. Cross-language search supported. Read-only operation. Use when the user asks about project documentation, notes, reference material, or anything stored in their knowledge base rather than personal memories.

tools.name: recall_all
tools.description: Unified search across BOTH personal memories (from recall_memories) AND knowledge base (from recall_from_knowledge) simultaneously. Merges and deduplicates results from both sources. Useful when the user's query could match either personal memories OR documentation/knowledge. Returns combined results with source indicator ('memory' or 'knowledge') for each entry. Read-only operation. Use this as the default search when unsure which source to query.

tools.name: declare_preference
tools.description: Explicitly declare a user preference without going through classification. Bypasses the classifier and directly stores as type=user_preference with high confidence. Use when the user explicitly says things like 'I prefer X', 'My default is Y', 'Always do Z' — statements that are unambiguously preferences. Faster than classify_and_remember because it skips classification step. NOT idempotent if the same preference already exists (creates version history). Returns {status, type, key, content}.

tools.name: get_memory_profile
tools.description: Return the complete user identity profile (whoami). Aggregates all stored memories into a structured profile grouped by type: preferences (⭐), corrections (🔧), decisions (🎯), facts (📌), relationships (❓), tasks (🔄), sentiments (💭). Includes statistics: total count, dominant type, average confidence, last activity. This is what gets injected into system prompts. Read-only operation. Use when you need to summarize who the user is, generate an introduction, or check current preference state.

tools.name: get_system_prompt
tools.description: Build a complete AI system prompt with relevant memories injected according to context. Selects memories matching the current namespace/topic, applies scope-aware injection (only injects relevant preferences for the current context), respects token budget (60% allocated to preferences, never truncated), and formats output as ready-to-use system prompt string. Returns the prompt text with injection summary (how many memories injected, token count). Read-only and idempotent (same input produces same prompt). Use at the start of each conversation or when context changes to ensure AI has up-to-date user identity.

tools.name: summarize_and_store
tools.description: Summarize a long text (conversation transcript, article, document) into concise memory entries and store them. Extracts key points, decisions made, preferences expressed, and facts mentioned. Creates multiple memory entries from a single input. Useful for processing meeting transcripts, long conversations, or imported notes. NOT idempotent: running twice creates duplicate summaries (consolidate_memories can dedup later). Returns {entries_created, summary, original_length}.

tools.name: consolidate_memories
tools.description: Run memory consolidation pipeline to clean up and optimize stored memories. Three phases: P0 (deduplication via Jaccard similarity + exponential decay of old memories), P1 (pattern detection → promote repeated patterns to rule candidates), P2 (semantic clustering → merge related memories via LLM). Preferences are NEVER decayed or deduplicated. By default runs dry_run=True (preview only, no changes). Set run_p1=True/run_p2=True for deeper consolidation. Returns report with {duplicates_found, to_decay, candidates_promoted, stats}. Expensive operation for large databases. Use periodically (weekly) or when memory quality degrades.

tools.name: schedule_consolidation
tools.description: Schedule automatic background consolidation to run at a fixed interval using threading.Timer. After scheduling, consolidation runs automatically every N hours without manual intervention. Only ONE schedule can be active at a time; calling again replaces the previous schedule. Returns {scheduled: True, interval_hours, next_run}. Use for set-and-forget maintenance. Pair with stop_consolidation to cancel. Note: process must remain running for scheduled consolidation to execute.

tools.name: stop_consolidation
tools.description: Cancel an active automatic consolidation schedule started by schedule_consolidation. If no schedule is active, returns gracefully with {scheduled: False}. Idempotent: safe to call even if nothing is scheduled. Returns {cancelled: True, was_scheduled: Boolean}.

tools.name: add_rule
tools.description: Create a new behavioral rule that will be automatically matched and injected into future prompts. Rules have: trigger pattern (when it applies), rule body (what to inject), scope (which contexts), type (preference/correction/constraint/avoidance), and priority. Example: trigger='database', body='Use PostgreSQL', scope=['coding'], type='preference'. NOT idempotent: adding the same rule twice creates duplicates (check with list_rules first). Returns {status, rule_id, trigger, body}. Use when the user wants to establish persistent behavioral patterns beyond individual memories.

tools.name: list_rules
tools.description: List all stored rules or filter by criteria (status, type, scope, keyword). Returns array of rules with {id, trigger, body, scope, type, priority, created_at, match_count, active_status}. Supports pagination via limit/offset. Read-only operation. Use to review current rule set, check for conflicts, or verify a specific rule exists before adding.

tools.name: match_rules
tools.description: Find all rules that match a given context string or user message. Evaluates each active rule's trigger pattern against the input. Returns matched rules sorted by priority (highest first) with {id, trigger, body, matched_by, relevance_score}. Used internally by get_system_prompt but can be called directly for debugging or preview. Read-only and idempotent. Use to show the user which rules would apply to their current context before injecting them.

tools.name: inject_rules
tools.description: Take matched rules and format them into injectable prompt text. Applies template formatting, scope filtering, and conflict resolution. Called automatically by get_system_prompt but available separately for custom injection workflows. Returns formatted text block ready for system prompt insertion. Read-only (does not modify rules). Use when building custom prompts with rule injection outside the standard get_system_prompt flow.

tools.name: my_rules
tools.description: Quick view of the user's currently active rules in human-readable format. Returns a summarized list showing trigger patterns and rule bodies, grouped by type (preference/correction/constraint/avoidance). Includes total count and last-updated timestamp. Convenience shortcut equivalent to list_rules(status='active'). Read-only. Use when the user asks 'what rules do I have?' or 'show my rules'.

tools.name: delete_rule
tools.description: Permanently delete a rule by its ID. Destructive operation: cannot be undone (though rules are typically simple enough to recreate). Returns boolean success. Use with caution — confirm the rule ID before deleting. Use when a rule is outdated, incorrect, or no longer needed.

tools.name: suggest_rules
tools.description: Analyze stored memories to detect repeated patterns and suggest new candidate rules. Looks for: frequently occurring preferences (>3 similar statements), consistent corrections (same mistake corrected repeatedly), and recurring decisions. Returns array of suggested rules with {trigger, body, confidence, evidence_count, source_memories}. Does NOT create rules — user must explicitly accept via promote_rules. Read-only analysis operation. Use proactively when many memories have accumulated to help user discover implicit patterns.

tools.name: promote_rules
tools.description: Promote one or more candidate rules (from suggest_rules output) to active status. Converts suggestions into real rules that will be matched and injected. Accepts list of suggestion IDs or rule definitions. Returns {promoted_count, rule_ids, failures}. Use after reviewing suggestions from suggest_rules to make them permanent.

tools.name: update_rule
tools.description: Modify an existing rule's properties (trigger, body, scope, type, priority). Partial update: only specified fields are changed; others preserved. Returns {status, updated_fields, rule_id}. Use to refine rules that are too broad, too narrow, or have outdated triggers. NOT idempotent for trigger/body changes (creates new version in some implementations).

tools.name: my_profile
tools.description: Comprehensive user identity profile combining memories, rules, and preferences into a single structured output. More detailed than get_memory_profile — includes active rules, preference summary, recent activity timeline, and statistics. Returns {identity: {preferences, corrections, decisions, facts}, rules: [...], stats: {...}, timeline: [...]}. Read-only operation. Use for complete user context dump, export, or deep introspection.

tools.name: onboard
tools.description: Start the new-user onboarding flow. Accepts name, role, initial preferences, and optional namespace. Creates initial memory entries for the user's declared identity, sets up default preferences, and establishes baseline profile. Idempotent for the same user (updates existing onboard data). Best practice: call once per user/namespace during first interaction. Returns {status, user_created, preferences_set, profile_snapshot}. Use when meeting a new user or setting up CarryMem for the first time.

tools.name: health_check
tools.description: Check CarryMem system health. Returns adapter health, audit logger stats, memory count, and uptime. Lightweight check that does not start any HTTP service — use this from MCP clients to verify CarryMem is operational. Read-only and idempotent.
